extracted.intended_audience: practicing patent litigators, judges, and law students studying patent infringement litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary/procedural guidance for asserting and defending against enumerated statutory and equitable defenses in U.S. patent infringement actions, and for conducting patent trials (jury, bench, depositions, referees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighteenth defence — prior patent of same inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires introduction in evidence of the prior patent granted on the application of the same inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seldom requires expert testimony because the prior claim must be so clearly co-extensive with the claim in suit that co-extensiveness is apparent on the faces of the two patents; however expert testimony may be necessary where one or both claims are in phraseology that cannot be understood without expert explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nineteenth defence — court record repealing the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires support by the introduction of an officially attested copy of the record of the court repealing the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record is proved destroyed or illegible and not restored, it may be proved by a witness who examined and copied it when intact. Parol evidence is not admitted if only part of a record is lost — the existing part must be produced or proved by officially attested copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twentieth defence — foreign patent to curtail term
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires a properly certified copy of the foreign patent relied upon to curtail the term of the U.S. patent in suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties offer no testimony, the court will determine whether the foreign patent is for the same invention by inspection of the documents; expert evidence on this subject will be received. A foreign patent is evidence of its own duration and will be held not extended absent evidence to the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-first defence — unmarked sale/making of patented article
rubrics_metrics.description: Supported by proof that plaintiff made or sold specimens of the patented article without marking them 'patented', together with the day and year the patent was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introduced, the burden shifts to plaintiff (if accounting is prayed) to show defendant was duly notified before suit and continued infringing after notice. Voluntary statements by third persons that doings infringe are not statutory notice. Defence does not apply to process patents (processes are used not made or sold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-second defence — attack on plaintiff's title
rubrics_metrics.description: May be sustained by pointing out faults in plaintiff's proof of title by introducing intervening assignments or grants in writing that impair continuity of the chain of title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No title will be recognized in a court of law unless evidenced by instruments in writing; numerous legal points on title are treated elsewhere (eleventh chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-third defence — license (written/parol, express/implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: May be sustained by evidence of a written or parol license, or of an express or implied license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license may be a defense even where the license fee is in arrears. Further details on the proper evidence to support this defence are in the twelfth chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-fourth defence — release (total or partial)
rubrics_metrics.description: May be sustained by proof of a total or partial release given after the infringement and before the action, or pro tanto by a partial release given after the action began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper cannot be a release if executed before the infringement occurred. Whether a release given only to a joint infringer operates to release co-infringers depends on enforceability of contribution between infringers; where contribution is enforceable, a full release to one may release all. A release by one co-owner to an infringer is not a defense to actions by other co-owners against that infringer (it will only bar damages due to releasing co-owner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-fifth defence — non-infringement (burden and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may prevail on non-infringement and sometimes without evidence if plaintiff fails to prove infringement; but when plaintiff makes a prima facie case, defendant generally should introduce evidence of non-infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant's evidence may include expert testimony acquainted with the patent and defendant's doings, stating opinion that defendant's doings are substantially different and giving intelligent reasons. Expert testimony must describe defendant's doings to allow court comparison. Expert opinions are often based on hypothetical constructions and may be disregarded if judge finds hypotheticals erroneous. Defendant need not disclose secret process if he can prove omitted steps; conformity to a junior patent is admissible to show non-infringement (law settled affirmatively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of conformity to a junior patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether defendant's conformity to a junior patent is admissible to show non-infringement of the senior patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court decisions vacillated but ultimately held the point affirmatively (as of 1895); lower courts have uniformly followed that decision since. Thus evidence that defendant conformed to a junior patent may tend to show non-infringement of the patent in suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-sixth defence — estoppel (proof as pleaded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires proof as pleaded; estoppel in pais may be proved by parol or documents, estoppel by deed requires production of the deed, estoppel by record or res judicata must be proved according to rules for such evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record proved stops short of showing that the issue was decided in the former case, that fact may be proved by extrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-seventh defence — statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually requires little evidence because Federal courts take judicial notice of statutes of limitation and plaintiff's pleadings/proofs generally show when the infringement was committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff's presentation leaves the time of infringement uncertain enough to affect the limitation question, burden shifts to defendant to prove that part or all of the infringement is time-barred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-eighth defence — illegal acts by Patent Office/record production
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally requires production of the record of the patent application together with proof of whatever acts of the Commissioner are relied upon as illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defence relies on official records and proof of the Commissioner's acts; produce application record and supporting proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony — modes and formalities (depositions and oral testimony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in patent infringement actions may be taken orally in open court or by depositions in writing under specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositions allowed where witness lives more than 100 miles from trial, is bound on a voyage, is about to go out of U.S. or judicial district, or is ancient/infirm; certain magistrates may take depositions (U.S. judges, state court judges, commissioners, clerks, mayors, notaries) unless disqualified. Reasonable written notice stating witness name, time and place is required. Formalities prescribed in Revised Statutes sections must be strictly complied with; depositions are inadmissible unless witness is dead, gone out of U.S., >100 miles away, or unable to travel by reason of age, sickness, infirmity or imprisonment. Depositions may be taken in modes prescribed by state laws in some instances. Translation permitted where witness cannot testify in English. Most objections to depositions must be made before receipt; evidence admitted with acquiescence cannot later be excluded on procedural ground. Evidence admitted but pertinent only to unpleaded defenses cannot be used to support those unpleaded defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's directed verdict (when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge may direct a verdict for the defendant where it is entirely clear the plaintiff cannot recover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction may be given where want of novelty or invention is clearly shown by a prior patent, but not where the question is doubtful. Direction may be given where infringement depends entirely on construction of the patent and that construction does not depend upon any doubtful question of prior art. If construction depends on doubtful prior art, the question should be left to the jury. Motion for directed verdict need not specify reason but that reason is stated in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions to jury in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions set forth the construction of patents and embody law applicable to material facts in evidence, but need not include other law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges consult statutes and Supreme Court decisions and may use Circuit Court of Appeals and lower court decisions as needed. Judges are not bound by obiter dicta unless applicable to the case. Text-writers' statements may be followed. Instructions may express judge's opinions but should not enforce them; should not include reading of charge from another case. Judge tells jury what issues of fact (from the pleadings) they must decide. In federal courts, instructions may be given orally or in writing at the court's option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent verdict rules — when plaintiff entitled to verdict
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff entitled to verdict if every defense except non-infringement fails and non-infringement fails as to any one claim; similar rules for combinations of partial defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If some defenses succeed only against part of alleged infringement or part of claims, plaintiff may still be entitled to verdict as to the residue. Specific combinations (e.g., 16th–18th defences) described where plaintiff still entitled to verdict if those defences lack application to one or more claims shown violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and limits for new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: New trial may be obtained if jury disregarded instructions or failed to correctly apply them, subject to limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A wrong decision alone does not warrant new trial unless against weight of evidence. Excessive damages may be cured by plaintiff's remittitur where judge thinks excess arose from inadvertence; new trial granted where error arose from prejudice or reckless disregard. Errors by judge entitle party to new trial only if excepted to at the time, and not if subsequent trial rendered error nugatory. Erroneous instructions on damages may be avoided by consenting to reduce verdict to nominal damages and costs. Newly discovered evidence may be grounds for new trial if it could not with due diligence have been obtained before and is not merely cumulative; moving party must succeed on strength of his affidavits vs opposing affidavits; usual terms require payment of former trial costs by appellant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bench trial (judge without jury) — findings and appeal implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials by judge without jury must distinguish issues of law and fact; findings have different reviewability consequences depending on general or special findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General findings are conclusive on facts and on questions of law except those arising upon the pleadings or specified in bill of exceptions. Special findings are conclusive on facts found but sufficiency of those facts to support judgment is open to review. If judge simply finds for defendant and enters judgment, review in Circuit Court of Appeals is by bill of exceptions and writ of error only on pure questions of law. Examples: judge's findings that patent void for want of novelty or no infringement support judgment but may be reversed if appellate court disagrees with sufficiency of facts found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by referee — procedure and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Case may be referred by clerk entry or by written stipulation; referee hears parties, decides controversy and makes report (special or general) to court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either party may except in writing to the report; court may adopt, reject, or recommit with directions. Trial by referee is regulated by state law (not provided by U.S. statute) so rules on taking testimony before referees, report timing, weight of reports, and practice for review are governed by the law of the state where trial occurs.
